title: Electrostatic Stabilization of Near-Surface Quantum Sensors via Dielectric Interface Engineering
authors: Atharva Paranjape, Kathrin Küster, Olga Shevstova, Lisa Ebo, Toni Hache, Klaus Kern, Rainer Stöhr, Jörg Wrachtrup, Aparajita Singha
abstract: Control of charge-state stability in near-surface quantum defects is critical for nanoscale sensing, yet remains particularly challenging under ultra-high vacuum (UHV), where surface-induced band bending destabilizes the metrologically relevant charge-state. Here, we present a robust and reproducible approach for stabilizing shallowly implanted (< 10 nm deep) nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in near-UHV conditions (P = $3 \times 10^{-9}$ mbar) based on dielectric interface engineering. Through measurements on individually addressable NV centers, we demonstrate that a TiO2 coating on the diamond suppresses surface-induced electrostatic fields, yielding a 79% increase n NV- population and a 45% enhancement in NV-spin resonance contrast at room temperature. Coherent control measurements further reveal suppressed charge-state conversion dynamics. These results establish dielectric screening as a powerful and reproducible strategy to engineer charge transition energetics of NV centers in scanning-probe-compatible geometries under extreme conditions.
summary: This paper demonstrates a method to stabilize charge states in shallow NV centers within diamond by coating the surface with a dielectric TiO2 layer. By suppressing surface-induced electric fields, the coating significantly boosts the concentration of the desired NV- charge state and enhances the sensor's magnetic resonance contrast. This establishes dielectric engineering as a powerful tool for robust quantum sensing under extreme vacuum conditions.
main_problem: Controlling the charge-state stability of near-surface quantum defects, like NV centers, is crucial for nanoscale sensing, especially in ultra-high vacuum where surface effects cause instability.
main_result: Applying a TiO2 dielectric coating suppresses detrimental surface-induced electrostatic fields, leading to a significant increase in the stable NV- charge state and enhancing spin resonance contrast.
method: The researchers used Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) to deposit a TiO2 coating on diamond, followed by fluorescence and optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) measurements under near-UHV conditions.
model_or_system: The system involves Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers implanted shallowly (< 10 nm) in diamond. The key physics revolves around the charge-state equilibrium between NV- and NV0, which dictates the sensor's performance.
key_observables: NV- charge state fraction (quantified via fluorescence spectroscopy), ODMR spin resonance contrast, and spin coherence dynamics (Rabi oscillations).
important_parameters: Near-UHV pressure ($3 	imes 10^{-9}$ mbar), room temperature (300 K), and the dielectric coating material (TiO2).
main_assumptions: The measured charge-state fraction (c-) is used as a reliable proxy for the actual stable NV- population, and the coating process itself does not introduce significant bulk defects.
figures_summary: Figures compare fluorescence spectra and ODMR measurements before and after TiO2 coating, showing quantitative improvements in charge-state stability and contrast. Rabi oscillation measurements confirm preserved coherent control.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (surface instability) and proposes the solution (dielectric engineering). It presents characterization (XPS, fluorescence) to quantify the improvement, followed by advanced measurements (ODMR, Rabi oscillations) to demonstrate enhanced sensing capability.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental blueprint for mitigating environmental decoherence sources (surface electric fields) in solid-state quantum memories, which is highly relevant for building robust quantum sensors and quantum computing platforms.
